name: The First Life (Stromatolites)
scope: Layered mounds still built by cyanobacteria in Shark Bay, Australia are living copies of the oldest fossils of life — Australian stromatolites ~3.5 billion years old, evidence life existed for most of Earth's history before animals.
source: Britannica (stromatolites); NHM London; Australian Shark Bay / Pilbara records
framing_note: Scene-led: the living Shark Bay mounds are the visual handle, not a bare date. Standard science stated plainly (~3.5 billion years); the payoff answer is the NAMED THING (stromatolites / cyanobacteria), never a cold number.

name: The Great Oxygenation Event
scope: The first great poisoning: ~2.4 billion years ago cyanobacteria pumped out oxygen as waste, rusting the oceans (banded iron formations) and killing most life that couldn't tolerate it — the atmosphere animals would later breathe was pollution first.
source: Britannica; NHM London; banded iron formation literature
framing_note: Frame as the paradox — oxygen as a mass poison that reshaped the planet. Standard science; the memorable payoff is the concept (waste oxygen / the rusting oceans / banded iron), with 2.4 billion years only as constructed context.

name: The Three Great Eras
scope: The deep-time map every kid needs: Paleozoic (age of old life, ~542-252M), Mesozoic (age of dinosaurs, 252-66M), Cenozoic (age of mammals, 66M-now) — and the two great extinctions that punctuate the boundaries.
source: Britannica; International Commission on Stratigraphy chart
framing_note: Anchor each era to its living cast (old life / dinosaurs / mammals), not the raw dates — a bare era name as answer is banned unless the stem builds drama to it. Standard science; correct current boundary ages.

name: The Cambrian Explosion
scope: ~540M years ago, in a geological blink (~25M years), nearly every major animal body plan alive today first appears in the rock — eyes, shells, legs, guts erupt at once; the moment the animal kingdom's blueprints were drawn.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Cambrian explosion literature
framing_note: Sell the suddenness and the body-plan payoff (the phyla we still have), not a definition. Standard science. The answer should be the NAMED event or a vivid first-appearance, not the number 540M standing alone.

name: The Burgess Shale & Anomalocaris
scope: In 1909 Charles Walcott stumbled on a Canadian Rockies rock face preserving soft Cambrian bodies — the meter-long apex predator Anomalocaris with grasping face-claws, and five-eyed Opabinia with a nozzle-mouth; the strangest zoo in fossil history.
source: Britannica; Royal Ontario Museum Burgess Shale; Gould, Wonderful Life
framing_note: Lead with the alien creatures (Anomalocaris, Opabinia) as the named payoffs — Walcott and 1909 are context handles, not a cold 'who discovered' stem. Standard science; use current interpretation of Anomalocaris as a radiodont.

name: Trilobites
scope: The most successful animals ever fossilized — trilobites ruled the seas for ~270 million years, some with the first sophisticated eyes made of calcite crystal lenses, before vanishing utterly in the Permian Great Dying; the index fossil kids find first.
source: Britannica; NHM London; trilobite paleobiology literature
framing_note: Concrete handles: the crystal-lens eyes, the enrollment (rolling into a ball), the 270-million-year reign ending in the Great Dying. Standard science; the payoff is the named creature and its vivid feature, not a period boundary.

name: Devonian, the Age of Fishes
scope: 419-359M years ago the seas filled with fish, ruled by the armor-headed Dunkleosteus — a 6-tonne predator with no teeth but self-sharpening bony blades and one of the strongest bites ever measured; the period fish took over the world.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Dunkleosteus bite-force studies
framing_note: Anchor the period to Dunkleosteus's guillotine jaws rather than the date range. Standard science; the answer is the NAMED armored predator or its blade-jaws, not the bare period name.

name: Carboniferous Giant Insects
scope: 359-299M years ago, when oxygen hit ~35% of the air, insects grew monstrous — Meganeura, a dragonfly with a 70cm (2.3ft) wingspan, and Arthropleura, a 2.5m millipede; the coal-forest world of oxygen-fueled giants.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Carboniferous atmospheric-oxygen literature
framing_note: Lead with the seagull-sized dragonfly and car-length millipede; construct the high-oxygen cause as the payoff. Standard science. Named giants beat the period name; the O2 figure only as constructed context.

name: Dimetrodon, Not a Dinosaur
scope: The sail-backed Permian predator sold in every dinosaur toy set is NOT a dinosaur — Dimetrodon is a synapsid, closer to us than to any dinosaur, and lived and died tens of millions of years before the first dinosaur walked.
source: Britannica; NHM London; synapsid phylogeny literature
framing_note: Name the misconception directly — kids retell 'the sail-back isn't a dinosaur, it's on OUR branch.' Standard science; the payoff is the synapsid/mammal-ancestor reveal, correct taxonomy (do not call it a reptile in the dinosaur sense).

name: The Gorgonopsians
scope: Before dinosaurs, saber-toothed predators already ruled — Permian gorgonopsians like Inostrancevia were mammal-relatives (not reptiles) with true saber fangs, the first great fanged killers, wiped out in the Great Dying.
source: Britannica; NHM London; therapsid literature
framing_note: The wonder hook: sabertooths existed 200M years before Smilodon and were on the mammal branch. Standard science; correct therapsid/synapsid framing, real genus names only.

name: Tiktaalik, the Fishapod
scope: Neil Shubin bet evolution was predictable: he searched 375-million-year-old Devonian rock on Ellesmere Island because that was where and when a fish-to-land transitional SHOULD be — and in 2004 found Tiktaalik, a fish with a neck, wrists, and proto-limbs.
source: Shubin, Your Inner Fish; UChicago Biological Sciences; Nature 2006; Tiktaalik.uchicago.edu
framing_note: The prediction is the wow — Shubin picked the rock's age and place, then the fossil showed up. Standard science stated confidently. Discovered 2004, published 2006, ~375M; answer is the NAMED fishapod and the successful prediction, not a date.

name: The Five Mass Extinctions
scope: Life has been nearly erased five times — the Big Five (Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic, K-Pg) — and the Permian 'Great Dying' was the worst of all, the yardstick every other catastrophe is measured against.
source: Britannica; Raup & Sepkoski Big Five; NHM London
framing_note: Frame as a countdown to the worst rather than a list to memorize. Standard science; the payoff answer is 'the Permian / the Great Dying' constructed as the champion of catastrophe, not a bare period name.

name: The Permian Great Dying
scope: 252M years ago Siberian Traps volcanism cooked the planet and killed ~95% of all marine species and ~70% of land species — life came within a whisker of ending; the closest Earth ever came to a lifeless ocean.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Siberian Traps / end-Permian literature
framing_note: Build the stem toward the 95% payoff so the number LANDS as a gut-punch (constructed, not cold). Standard science; name the Siberian Traps as cause. 'The Great Dying' is a legitimate named-thing answer.

name: The Triassic-Jurassic Extinction
scope: ~201M years ago a fourth catastrophe cleared the big crocodile-relatives that had dominated the land — and the survivors, the dinosaurs, exploded into the empty world to rule the next 135 million years.
source: Britannica; NHM London; end-Triassic (CAMP volcanism) literature
framing_note: Frame as the door that opened FOR dinosaurs — the payoff is the dinosaur radiation, not the date. Standard science; note the extinction cleared rival archosaurs, enabling dinosaur dominance.

name: The Day the Dinosaurs Died (K-Pg / Chicxulub)
scope: 66M years ago a 10-km asteroid slammed into the Yucatán at Chicxulub, ending the non-avian dinosaurs. Deep ladder: Walter & Luis Alvarez's 1980 iridium-layer clue (metal from space in a global clay band), the 1991 crater confirmation, the ~180km crater buried under Mexico, the impact winter, and that BIRDS are the dinosaurs that survived.
source: Britannica; Alvarez et al. 1980 Science; NHM London; Chicxulub crater literature
framing_note: Keystone ladder — include accessible T2 base rungs (asteroid hit the dinosaurs) climbing to the Alvarez iridium detective story at T4-T5. Standard science stated confidently; birds ARE surviving theropod dinosaurs. Named things (Chicxulub, the iridium layer, the Alvarezes) beat dates.

name: Chicxulub vs. the Deccan Traps
scope: Did the asteroid alone kill the dinosaurs, or was the planet already reeling from the Deccan Traps — colossal volcanic eruptions in India spewing gas for hundreds of thousands of years around the same 66M-year mark? Scientists still argue the relative blame.
source: Britannica; Deccan Traps / K-Pg debate literature (Renne, Keller, Schoene)
framing_note: Present the live scientific debate honestly — impact vs. volcanism contribution is genuinely unsettled among researchers. NOT a moral-contested topic, so vision_mandated stays false, but frame both hypotheses fairly without a verdict. Standard science otherwise.

name: Tyrannosaurus rex
scope: Late Cretaceous (68-66M) North America's apex predator — ~12m, banana-sized serrated teeth, a bite that could crush bone (the strongest of any land animal ever), forward-facing eyes for binocular vision, and tiny but powerfully muscled arms. Deep ladder from the base fact up to bite-force and growth science.
source: Britannica; NHM London; AMNH; T. rex bite-force / growth-curve studies
framing_note: Base T2 rungs give the iconic predator; climb to bone-crushing bite force and binocular vision. ALWAYS 'T. rex' or 'Tyrannosaurus rex' — never 'T. Rex'. Standard science; feathers on tyrannosaurs are debated, so hedge honestly rather than asserting.

name: Triceratops
scope: Three horns, a great bony frill, and one of the last dinosaurs standing — Triceratops shared the Late Cretaceous with T. rex, and healed puncture wounds on fossil frills hint the two actually fought.
source: Britannica; NHM London; ceratopsian literature
framing_note: Scene-led: the horns-vs-tyrant showdown and the healed frill wounds are the payoffs. Standard science; frill function (display/defense/thermoregulation) is debated — present as open, don't assert armor.

name: The Real Velociraptor
scope: Jurassic Park lied: the real Velociraptor was turkey-sized (~2m nose-to-tail, waist-high), and a quill-knob fossil proves it was covered in FEATHERS — the movie's scaly monster is a fantasy.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Turner et al. 2007 (quill knobs on Velociraptor)
framing_note: Bust the movie myth head-on — the feathered turkey-sized reality is the dinner-table payoff. Standard science; feathers confirmed via quill knobs. The 'raptors' of the films were closer in size to Deinonychus, worth noting.

name: Stegosaurus's Plates
scope: The back plates were probably NOT armor — too thin and full of blood vessels — but display and heat-shedding radiators; the real weapon was the spiked tail (the 'thagomizer'), and Stegosaurus had a brain the size of a walnut.
source: Britannica; NHM London; stegosaur plate-vascularization literature
framing_note: Correct the armor misconception; the spiked-tail 'thagomizer' (a Far Side joke that became real terminology) is a great retellable handle. Standard science; plate function still discussed, present as best-supported not settled.

name: Brontosaurus Is Back
scope: 'Brontosaurus' was declared a mistake in 1903 (lumped into Apatosaurus) and every kid was told it never existed — but a huge 2015 study by Emanuel Tschopp resurrected it as a valid genus after all. The thunder lizard is real again.
source: Tschopp et al. 2015 PeerJ; NHM London (Brontosaurus reinstating); Britannica
framing_note: The reinstatement is the payoff — kids love that a 'wrong' dinosaur came back. CURRENT taxonomy required: Brontosaurus is a valid genus again as of 2015. Standard science; name Tschopp, real study.

name: Spinosaurus, the Swimming Dinosaur
scope: Bigger than T. rex and built to swim — Spinosaurus had a crocodile snout, a sail on its back, and a 2020 Moroccan fossil revealed a paddle-shaped tail for underwater propulsion; the first non-bird dinosaur shown adapted to hunt in water.
source: Ibrahim et al. 2014 & 2020 Nature; National Geographic; NHM London
framing_note: The paddle-tail reveal is the wonder payoff. Standard science; note the aquatic degree is still actively debated (2020 paddle-tail vs. 2022 counterarguments) — present the swimming adaptation as strongly supported but the extent as discussed.

name: Argentinosaurus, the Largest Dinosaur
scope: The biggest animal ever to walk the land — Argentinosaurus, a Cretaceous Argentine titanosaur ~35m long and ~75 tonnes, weighing more than a dozen elephants, known from vertebrae as tall as a person.
source: Britannica; titanosaur size-estimate literature; Museo Carmen Funes
framing_note: Sell the scale with a concrete handle (a-dozen-elephants, person-tall vertebrae). Standard science; note size is estimated from fragmentary remains — hedge 'among the largest' honestly. The named titan beats the tonnage number.

name: Feathered Dinosaurs of Liaoning
scope: In the 1990s, Chinese farmers in Liaoning Province began pulling out dinosaurs with FEATHERS preserved in ash — Sinosauropteryx with its ginger-and-white striped tail (the first dinosaur whose real color we know), and four-winged Microraptor; proof feathers came before flight.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Liaoning / Jehol Biota literature; Sinosauropteryx melanosome studies
framing_note: Named feathered dinosaurs (Sinosauropteryx, Microraptor) are the payoffs; the recovered ginger stripe color is the killer retell. Standard science stated confidently — feathered dinosaurs are settled, birds are theropods.

name: Archaeopteryx, the First Bird
scope: Found in 1861 in a German limestone quarry just as Darwin's book was fresh, Archaeopteryx had feathers and wings like a bird but teeth, claws, and a bony tail like a dinosaur — the fossil that put a face on the transition, found the year evolution needed it most.
source: Britannica; NHM London (Archaeopteryx); Solnhofen limestone literature
framing_note: The timing (1861, just after Darwin) plus the teeth-and-feathers mosaic is the payoff. Standard science; present as a transitional theropod-bird. Named creature over date.

name: The Age of Sharks (Megalodon)
scope: The largest shark that ever lived, Otodus megalodon, cruised the seas until ~3.6M years ago — teeth the size of a human hand, a body estimated up to ~18m, a bite that could crush a whale's ribcage; known almost entirely from its teeth because shark skeletons are cartilage.
source: Britannica; NHM London; megalodon body-size / bite-force literature
framing_note: The hand-sized teeth and cartilage-not-bone fact are the retellable handles. Standard science; body-size estimates are uncertain (from teeth/vertebrae) — hedge. Do NOT imply it coexisted with dinosaurs; it's Cenozoic.

name: Sarcosuchus, the SuperCroc
scope: A Cretaceous crocodile relative the length of a bus — Sarcosuchus, ~12m and up to ~8 tonnes, with a snout built to ambush dinosaurs at the water's edge; the giant croc that ate dinosaurs.
source: Britannica; Sereno et al. Sarcosuchus literature; National Geographic 'SuperCroc'
framing_note: The bus-length croc that hunted dinosaurs is the wonder hook. Standard science; note it's a crocodilian relative (pseudosuchian), not a true modern crocodile. Named creature payoff.

name: Quetzalcoatlus, the Giant Pterosaur
scope: The largest flying animal ever — Quetzalcoatlus, a Cretaceous pterosaur with a ~10-11m wingspan (a small plane) that stood as tall as a giraffe on the ground and stalked prey on foot; and a reminder pterosaurs were NOT dinosaurs.
source: Britannica; NHM London; azhdarchid pterosaur literature
framing_note: Giraffe-tall / small-plane wingspan are the concrete handles. Standard science; explicitly note pterosaurs are flying archosaurs, NOT dinosaurs (common misconception, name it). Named creature over span number.

name: Mosasaurs & Plesiosaurs, Sea Monsters
scope: The seas of the dinosaur age had their own giants that were NOT dinosaurs — mosasaurs, giant marine lizards related to today's monitor lizards, and long-necked plesiosaurs like the one Mary Anning first pulled from the cliffs.
source: Britannica; NHM London; marine-reptile literature
framing_note: The correction that sea reptiles weren't dinosaurs is a good payoff; tie plesiosaurs forward to the Anning ladder. Standard science, correct taxonomy (mosasaurs = squamates near monitors).

name: Morganucodon, Among the First Mammals
scope: While dinosaurs ruled, our ancestors were shrew-sized and nocturnal — Morganucodon (~205M years ago) was mouse-small, insect-eating, and among the earliest mammals; mammals spent 135 million years small and hiding before their chance came.
source: Britannica; NHM London; early mammaliaform literature
framing_note: The 'our ancestors hid in the dark for 135 million years' framing is the payoff. Standard science; describe as an early mammaliaform/mammal. Concrete handle (mouse-sized, nocturnal) over jargon.

name: The Rise of the Mammals
scope: The moment the asteroid cleared the dinosaurs, placental mammals exploded to fill the empty world — from shrew-sized survivors to whales, bats, horses, and us, all within a few million years; the Cenozoic became the Age of Mammals.
source: Britannica; NHM London; eutherian post-K-Pg radiation literature
framing_note: Frame as the inheritance after the disaster — the payoff is the explosive radiation, not the term 'eutherian'. Standard science stated confidently.

name: Whales Walked on Land (Pakicetus)
scope: The blue whale's ancestor had legs and lived on land — Pakicetus (~50M, dog-sized, hoofed) walked riverbanks in Pakistan, then Ambulocetus ('walking whale') took to the water, Rodhocetus's legs shrank, and the fossil series shows the whole march from shore to sea; whales still have vestigial hip bones.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Thewissen / Gingerich cetacean-transition literature
framing_note: Keystone transitional ladder — the named intermediates (Pakicetus, Ambulocetus, Rodhocetus) and the vestigial hip bones are the payoffs. Standard science stated confidently: whales descended from land mammals, one of the best-documented transitions.

name: Birds ARE Dinosaurs
scope: The chickadee at the feeder is a living theropod dinosaur — the wishbone, hollow bones, three-fingered hand, feathers, and a special half-moon wrist bone (the semilunate carpal) that let raptors fold their arms are all inherited straight from dinosaurs; dinosaurs never fully went extinct.
source: Britannica; NHM London; theropod-bird phylogeny literature
framing_note: The 'dinosaurs are still alive at your bird feeder' payoff is core wonder. Standard science stated confidently and plainly — not hedged. Concrete shared traits (wishbone, semilunate wrist) as handles.

name: The Woolly Mammoth
scope: The Ice Age icon — Mammuthus primigenius, curved 4m tusks, a fatty hump, found frozen with skin and stomach contents in Siberian permafrost. Deep ladder: the grazing giant, the frozen 'ice mummies', and the stunner that a holdout population survived on Wrangel Island until ~4,000 years ago — after the Great Pyramid was built.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Wrangel Island mammoth-survival literature
framing_note: Base T2 rung gives the iconic tusked grazer; climb to the Wrangel-outlived-the-pyramids gut-punch. Standard science; correct genus (Mammuthus). The 'younger than the pyramids' fact is the killer retell — constructed, not a cold date.

name: Mastodon vs. Mammoth
scope: Two shaggy elephants, one confusing name mix-up — the mastodon (Mammut) was a forest browser with cusped, cone-shaped teeth for crushing twigs, while the mammoth was an open-grassland grazer with washboard teeth; the teeth tell them apart, and they aren't even the same genus.
source: Britannica; NHM London; proboscidean tooth-morphology literature
framing_note: The tooth distinction (cone-cusped browser vs. washboard grazer) is the concrete payoff that resolves a common confusion. Standard science; different genus (Mammut vs Mammuthus).

name: Smilodon, the Sabertooth Cat
scope: The saber-toothed cat — Smilodon, with 18cm canines and a bear-like muscular build, killed with a precise throat bite (the fragile fangs couldn't take struggling prey). Deep ladder anchored on La Brea: thousands died trapped in the tar, and healed injuries in the bones hint they lived in social groups that cared for the hurt.
source: Britannica; La Brea Tar Pits / Page Museum; Smilodon paleobiology literature
framing_note: Base T2 gives the icon; climb to the throat-bite mechanics and La Brea social-behavior inference. Standard science; note 'sabertooth' is convergent — Smilodon is a true cat, unlike the Permian gorgonopsians. Named cat over the 18cm number.

name: La Brea Tar Pits
scope: In the middle of Los Angeles, sticky asphalt seeps trapped Ice Age animals for 50,000 years — dire wolves (over 4,000 individuals), sabertooths, mammoths, and giant condors — the richest Ice Age fossil site on Earth, still bubbling today.
source: La Brea Tar Pits / Natural History Museum of LA County; Britannica
framing_note: The 'Ice Age graveyard in downtown LA, still bubbling' image is the payoff that makes a kid want to visit. Standard science; the dire-wolf count is real and striking. Named place over dates.

name: The Giant Ground Sloth
scope: A sloth the size of an elephant — Megatherium, up to 6 tonnes, reared up on its hind legs to pull down whole tree branches with hooked claws; it lumbered across the Americas until ~10,000 years ago, and early humans may have met it.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Megatherium literature
framing_note: The elephant-sized sloth reaching into treetops is the wonder handle. Standard science; note it survived into human times in the Americas. Named creature over the tonnage.

name: The Short-Faced Bear
scope: The biggest land predator of Ice Age North America — Arctodus simus, so tall it could look a person in the eye on all fours and over 3.5m standing up, with long legs built for chasing across the open plains.
source: Britannica; Arctodus literature; La Brea Tar Pits
framing_note: The 'looks you in the eye on all fours' handle sells the scale. Standard science; note the long-legged running build (cursorial hunting is one hypothesis — present as proposed, not settled).

name: The Dire Wolf
scope: Real, not just Game of Thrones — the dire wolf was heavier-jawed than a gray wolf and hunted Ice Age megafauna, but a 2021 DNA study revealed it was so distinct it got a new genus, Aenocyon, and wasn't even a close cousin of true wolves.
source: Perri et al. 2021 Nature (Aenocyon reassignment); La Brea Tar Pits; Britannica
framing_note: The 2021 DNA reassignment is the payoff. CURRENT taxonomy required: reassigned to Aenocyon dirus in 2021, NOT a close relative of Canis lupus. Standard science; La Brea is the fossil source.

name: The Glyptodon
scope: A car-sized armadillo relative — Glyptodon carried a domed bony shell like a Volkswagen Beetle, and some relatives swung a spiked tail-club; early Americans may have sheltered under the empty shells. It survived to ~10,000 years ago.
source: Britannica; NHM London; glyptodont literature
framing_note: The VW-Beetle-with-a-shell and tail-club are the concrete handles. Standard science; a glyptodont (armadillo relative / xenarthran). Named creature over jargon.

name: The 'Irish Elk'
scope: Three misnomers in one name — Megaloceros was neither exclusively Irish nor an elk (it's a deer), and it grew the largest antlers of any animal ever, a 3.7m span weighing ~40kg, regrown every single year.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Megaloceros literature
framing_note: The 'not Irish, not an elk' triple-correction plus the record antlers is the retellable payoff. Standard science; it's a giant deer. Named creature and the antler-span handle over the raw numbers.

name: The Woolly Rhino & Cave Lion
scope: The Ice Age cast humans actually painted — the woolly rhino (Coelodonta) with a flat horn for sweeping snow off grass, and the cave lion, both drawn on the walls of Chauvet Cave 30,000+ years ago by people who hunted alongside them.
source: Britannica; Chauvet Cave art records; woolly rhino / cave lion literature
framing_note: Tie the animals to the Chauvet cave paintings — 'we have their portraits, drawn by people who saw them alive' is the payoff. Standard science; snow-sweeping horn use is inferred, present as such. Named creatures over dates.

name: Pleistocene Overkill vs. Climate
scope: Why did the mammoths, sabertooths, and giant sloths vanish ~13,000-10,000 years ago? Paul Martin's 1967 'overkill' hypothesis blames human hunters arriving and wiping them out fast; the rival view blames abrupt climate change at the Ice Age's end. Scientists still argue, and the answer likely differs by continent.
source: Paul Martin 1967 overkill; Britannica; late-Quaternary extinction debate literature (Barnosky, Koch & Barnosky)
framing_note: THE contested paleo topic — present BOTH sides fully and fairly, NO verdict. Attribute overkill to Paul Martin 1967; give the climate hypothesis equal, non-dismissive weight ('the overkill hypothesis argues...' vs '...misguidedly believe'). Wonder-led, not advocacy.

name: Mary Anning
scope: Self-taught and poor, struck by lightning as a baby and surviving it, Mary Anning combed the crumbling cliffs of Lyme Regis for a living and found deep time itself: the first ichthyosaur (age 12, 1811), the first complete plesiosaur (1823), the first British pterosaur (1828) — yet as a woman was barred from the scientific societies that used her finds.
source: NHM London (Mary Anning); Britannica; Lyme Regis Museum; Anning biographies
framing_note: Keystone human ladder — the poverty, the self-teaching, the lightning survival, and the named firsts (ichthyosaur/plesiosaur/pterosaur) are all payoffs; the exclusion-as-a-woman is the moral throughline. Standard science; real dates. Named finds over years.

name: The Bone Wars (Cope vs. Marsh)
scope: Two rich rivals, Edward Drinker Cope and Othniel Charles Marsh, spent the 1870s-90s racing to out-dig each other across the American West — bribing, spying, dynamiting sites so the other couldn't have them, and naming ~130 new dinosaurs (Triceratops, Stegosaurus, Allosaurus) while bankrupting and disgracing themselves. Marsh even put the wrong head on 'Brontosaurus'.
source: Britannica; NHM records; Bone Wars histories (Wallace, 'The Bonehunters' Revenge')
framing_note: Keystone story ladder — the sabotage, dynamiting, and the wrong-head-on-Brontosaurus are the dinner-table payoffs; name Cope and Marsh as the antagonists. Standard science; the dinosaurs they named are real. Named feud over dates.

name: Richard Owen & the Word 'Dinosaur'
scope: The man who coined 'Dinosauria' — 'terrible lizard' — in 1842 and built London's Natural History Museum as a cathedral to nature, Richard Owen was also Darwin's bitter enemy who fought evolution to the end; brilliant, ambitious, and not a nice man.
source: Britannica; NHM London (Richard Owen); Owen biographies
framing_note: The 'named the dinosaurs AND fought Darwin' tension is the payoff; the NHM as his monument makes it visitable. Standard science; note his anti-Darwin stance factually without editorializing beyond the record. Named coinage over the year.

name: Jack Horner & the Good-Mother Lizard
scope: In 1978 in Montana, Jack Horner found a whole hillside of dinosaur nests, eggs, and babies — Maiasaura, the 'good mother lizard' — proving some dinosaurs cared for their young in colonies; the discovery that turned dinosaurs from cold monsters into parents (and inspired Jurassic Park's advisor).
source: Britannica; Horner Maiasaura literature; Museum of the Rockies
framing_note: The nest-site reveal that gave dinosaurs parenting is the payoff; 'good mother lizard' is a perfect named handle. Standard science; Horner advised the Jurassic Park films (nice retellable aside). Named discovery over date.

name: Sue the T. rex
scope: In 1990 Sue Hendrickson found the largest, most complete T. rex ever in South Dakota — 90% of the skeleton — but a years-long ownership fight sent it to auction, where Chicago's Field Museum paid $8.36 million so Sue could stand on public display for good.
source: Field Museum (Sue); Britannica; Sue-auction records
framing_note: The completeness, the legal saga, and the record auction are the payoffs. 'T. rex' never 'T. Rex'. Standard science; named after finder Sue Hendrickson (the specimen's sex is unknown — note that). Named specimen over the price.

name: Lucy the Australopithecus
scope: In 1974 at Hadar, Ethiopia, Donald Johanson found ~40% of a 3.2-million-year-old skeleton — Australopithecus afarensis — proving our ancestors walked upright long before big brains evolved. The team named her Lucy because the Beatles' 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds' was playing at camp that night.
source: Britannica; Institute of Human Origins; Johanson 'Lucy'; NHM records
framing_note: Base T2 rung delivers the Beatles-song naming (pure dinner-table gold); climb to bipedalism-before-big-brains. Standard science stated confidently. Named fossil and the Beatles story over the date.

name: Sahelanthropus, the Oldest Hominin
scope: A ~7-million-year-old skull from Chad, nicknamed Toumaï ('hope of life'), sits near the very split between us and chimpanzees — possibly the oldest known member of the human line, though whether it walked upright is still fiercely argued.
source: Britannica; Sahelanthropus / Toumaï literature
framing_note: The 'oldest, right at the human-chimp split' framing plus the Toumaï nickname is the payoff. Standard science; be honest that its status and bipedality are debated — present as contested-within-science, not settled.

name: Homo habilis, the Handy Man
scope: ~2.4M years ago the first of our own genus, Homo habilis ('handy man'), started chipping sharp flakes off stones — the Oldowan tools, the oldest technology on Earth, that let a small-bodied ape cut meat it couldn't chew.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Oldowan / Homo habilis literature
framing_note: The 'first toolmaker, first of our genus' payoff with the Oldowan flake as concrete handle. Standard science; note habilis's status/definition is discussed, keep to well-supported claims. Named species over the date.

name: Homo erectus, Fire & the First Wanderer
scope: The first human ancestor to look like us from the neck down, Homo erectus made teardrop Acheulean hand axes, tamed fire, and was the first to walk out of Africa — spreading across Asia and surviving nearly two million years, longer than any human species yet.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Homo erectus literature
framing_note: The 'first out of Africa, tamed fire, outlasted us so far' payoffs. Standard science; controlled fire timing is debated (~1M+ BP claims contested) — hedge on the earliest dates. Named species over numbers.

name: Neanderthals
scope: Not brutish cavemen but skilled cold-adapted humans — Neanderthals buried their dead, made tools and pigments, cared for the injured, had bigger brains than us, and vanished ~40,000 years ago. The twist: they didn't fully die out — most people alive outside Africa carry ~2% Neanderthal DNA.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Pääbo Neanderthal genome; Reich lab introgression studies
framing_note: Bust the 'dumb caveman' myth, then land the '2% of your DNA is Neanderthal' payoff. Standard science stated confidently; the interbreeding is settled. Named species and the DNA fact over the extinction date.

name: The Denisovans
scope: A whole human species discovered from a single pinky bone — in a Siberian cave in 2008, a finger fragment's DNA (sequenced 2010) revealed the Denisovans, a lineage we knew almost nothing about anatomically, whose genes still help Tibetans breathe at altitude and live on in Melanesians.
source: Reich/Pääbo Denisova 2010 Nature; Britannica; Denisova Cave literature
framing_note: The 'entire species known first from a pinky bone and its DNA' is the wonder payoff; the Tibetan-altitude gene is the killer detail. Standard science; bone found 2008, DNA published 2010, ~4-6% in Melanesians. Named lineage over dates.

name: Homo sapiens Out of Africa
scope: Our own species is older than most think — ~300,000-year-old Homo sapiens fossils come from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco — and a later wave leaving Africa (~70,000-60,000 years ago) spread across the whole planet, meeting and mixing with Neanderthals and Denisovans along the way.
source: Britannica; Hublin Jebel Irhoud 2017; NHM London; Out-of-Africa literature
framing_note: The '300,000-year-old, older than you'd guess, and we mixed with the others' payoffs. Standard science stated confidently; Jebel Irhoud pushed the origin back. Named site/species over the dates.

name: Human Evolution Is a Bush, Not a Ladder
scope: The famous 'march of progress' image is wrong — human evolution isn't a straight line from ape to us. Multiple human species lived AT THE SAME TIME: as recently as ~50,000 years ago, Homo sapiens, Neanderthals, Denisovans, and the tiny 'hobbit' Homo floresiensis shared the planet. It's a branching bush, not a ladder.
source: Britannica; NHM London; Homo floresiensis literature; Gould on the bush metaphor
framing_note: NAME the misconception explicitly (the straight-line 'march of progress'). The 'four human species coexisted, including a hobbit' payoff. Standard science stated confidently. The bush-vs-ladder concept is the answer, not a date.

name: Anthropocene, the Human Age
scope: Have humans changed the planet enough to mark a new chapter in the rock? The proposed 'Anthropocene' epoch would be defined by a global layer — plastic, chicken bones, and plutonium fallout from 1950s nuclear tests — though geologists formally rejected it as an official epoch in 2024, and the debate continues.
source: Britannica; International Commission on Stratigraphy 2024 Anthropocene vote; Anthropocene Working Group
framing_note: The 'future fossil layer of plastic, chicken bones, and plutonium' is the vivid payoff. Present the formal status honestly as contested/rejected-as-formal-epoch (2024) but widely used informally. Wonder-led, no doom-preaching.

name: The Sixth Extinction (Kolbert)
scope: Elizabeth Kolbert's Pulitzer-winning 2014 book 'The Sixth Extinction' argues that after the Big Five, humans are now driving the sixth great die-off — told through vanishing species like the golden frog and the great auk, extinctions happening fast enough to read the rock of the future.
source: Kolbert 'The Sixth Extinction' 2014; Britannica; Pulitzer records
framing_note: The book and its Pulitzer are the named handles; make a kid want to read Kolbert (mirrors the 'want to visit La Brea' success bar). Standard science; the sixth-extinction framing is presented as her argument and mainstream concern, wonder-led not preachy.

name: The IUCN Red List
scope: The world's official scoreboard of endangerment — the IUCN Red List runs from Least Concern up through Vulnerable, Endangered, and Critically Endangered to Extinct in the Wild and Extinct; the ladder that tells us which animals are one step from gone.
source: IUCN Red List categories; Britannica
framing_note: Keep it about the ANIMALS and the severity ladder, not conservation-policy machinery (per animal.md §6). Standard science. Use a specific endangered creature as the scene handle so it's not a bare category list.

name: The Vanishing Amphibians (Chytrid)
scope: Frogs are dying worldwide from a skin fungus — chytrid (Bd) has driven ~90 amphibian species extinct and pushed hundreds more toward the edge, the deadliest wildlife disease ever recorded; the sixth extinction happening in real time to the animals kids catch in ponds.
source: Britannica; Scheele et al. 2019 Science (chytrid amphibian declines); IUCN
framing_note: Ground the sixth-extinction abstraction in a concrete, relatable creature (frogs) and cause (a fungus). Standard science; the chytrid death toll is real and striking. Keep it about the animal, not policy.
